segments: The Chronography of Barhebraeus.
[came] to the Persian and reproached him,
saying: 'How is it that you, while clad in mail together with all this armor that is with you,
fled from a single, stripped man and did not turn back to take his head?' But that Persian said to the soldier:
'Bring me a bolster.'
And when he brought it,
he shot an arrow into the bolster and pierced it, and said:
'So many times did I shoot in this manner at the Arab whom you saw,
and he brushed away all the arrows with his hands (cuffs) as if they were flies.'
And Yazdgerd gathered a second host again,
and he encountered the Arabs at the Euphrates.
And the Arabs were victorious,
and entered Ctesiphon,
and carried off its treasures and its people.
And again a third time he gathered [an army] in Jalula,
(footnote?)
and he encountered the Arabs,
and was defeated.
And again a fourth time he gathered [an army] in the mountains of Media,
and he encountered the Arabs,
and was broken.
These four assemblies took place in a single year.
And when this Yazdgerd lost hope,
he fled to the border of the Turks in the land of Sijistan.
And after five years that he was hidden there, he was killed,
and the kingdom of the Persians, which was called the House of Sasan, was brought to an end,
which had begun from Ardashir son of Babak in the year 538
of the Greeks (538),
and ended in the year 956.
He set out from Antioch for Constantinople, while saying:
'Sozo Syria!'
that is:
'Farewell, Syria!'
And he urged on his troops to plunder the Christians, the inhabitants of the country,
and more than the Arabs, the Romans themselves plundered everything they found.
And Heraclius wrote to Mesopotamia, Egypt, and Armenia to all the Romans:
'Let no man fight with the Arabs any longer,
except only that he who is able to keep his post
should remain in his place.'
And then 'Umar entered Egypt,
and Cyrus the bishop of Alexandria went out to meet him.
He agreed to give him two hundred thousand dinars every year,
and that the Arabs should not enter Egypt.
And 'Umar accepted,
and did not enter.
Now when Heraclius heard [this], he took offense, as if without constraint he was giving gold to the Arabs,
and he sent Manuel, an Armenian man, to take charge.
And when the envoys of the Arabs came to take the gold, Manuel said to them, while he was quartered with the army,
